what_its_for: Dextrose is a type of sugar (glucose) used to raise low blood sugar levels (hypoglycemia). It is also used to provide calories and energy when you cannot eat or drink normally. In the hospital, it may be given through an IV to keep your blood sugar in a safe range or to deliver other medicines.
how_to_take: Dextrose comes in several forms. Oral gels or tablets are taken by mouth and are used for low blood sugar emergencies. IV (intravenous) forms are given directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor in a hospital or clinic setting. Oral gels should be placed inside your cheek or under your tongue and allowed to absorb. For tablets, chew and swallow them with water. Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's exact instructions on how to use the form prescribed to you.
dosing: For low blood sugar episodes in adults and children over 2 years: oral glucose gels or tablets are usually given as 15 to 20 grams of glucose (about 3 to 4 glucose tablets or one tube of gel). Recheck your blood sugar after 15 minutes. If it is still low, repeat the dose. IV dosing is determined entirely by your doctor based on your blood sugar level, weight, and medical condition. Never adjust IV doses on your own. Always carry your prescribed dose with you if you are at risk for low blood sugar.
missed_dose: Dextrose is usually taken only when needed for low blood sugar or given continuously in the hospital. If you are using it on a scheduled basis and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your normal schedule. Never double up doses. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store oral glucose tablets and gels at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not freeze. Keep out of reach of children. Check the expiration date before use and throw away any expired products. IV dextrose solutions are stored and managed by healthcare professionals in a hospital setting.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking more dextrose than prescribed, as too much sugar can raise your blood sugar too high (hyperglycemia). If you have diabetes, avoid foods and drinks high in sugar right after treating low blood sugar unless directed by your doctor. Do not skip meals if you are at risk for low blood sugar. Avoid alcohol, as it can cause unpredictable changes in your blood sugar levels.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if: your blood sugar does not improve after taking dextrose twice in 15-minute intervals; you feel confused, have a seizure, or lose consciousness (call 911 immediately); you experience symptoms of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, or headache; you have swelling, redness, or pain at an IV site; you have signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Oral dextrose tablets or gels start raising your blood sugar within 10 to 15 minutes. You should begin to feel better (less shaky, sweaty, or confused) within 15 minutes of taking it. IV dextrose works very quickly, usually within a few minutes, because it goes directly into your bloodstream. Always recheck your blood sugar 15 minutes after treatment to make sure it has returned to a safe level.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Dextrose is generally considered safe during pregnancy when used as directed, but always inform your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Children: Dosing for children is based on weight and age; follow your doctor's instructions carefully. Elderly: Older adults may need closer monitoring as their blood sugar levels can change more quickly. Diabetics: People with diabetes should use dextrose only for treating confirmed low blood sugar episodes and should monitor blood sugar closely afterward. Kidney or liver disease: These conditions may affect how your body processes sugar, so your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely.
